explanations: terra: The punished Sabbath-breakers are made a deterrent example for those around and after them, precisely the section's sense of a penalty made exemplary so others recoil.

luna: The verse describes a slain man whose killing is disputed and concealed, then says God will bring what they conceal to light. This is a direct murder-investigation parallel to the section’s divided oath among a victim’s kin. | terra: A slain person and the community's dispute over the killing directly stage the concealed homicide and contested right that the section's family oaths seek to resolve.

luna: The next ayah commands an act involving the slain person and states that God gives life to the dead and shows signs; its own stated contribution is the sign of resurrection, completing the preceding murder-dispute scene without itself describing the kin’s oath. | terra: God exposes the murder of 2:72 by bringing the victim to life, so the hidden blood claim is answered by divine disclosure and a sign of resurrection.
luna: The warning says one soul cannot avail another and no ransom will be accepted, a boundary on what any human kin or guardian can accomplish at the final reckoning.

luna: The section reads the odd oath as kin seeking what is owed for a slain relative; this law prescribes qisas for the killed while allowing a brother to accept compensation and requiring fair payment. It gives that family claim a bounded legal course. | terra: This is the core family blood-claim scene: retaliation is prescribed for the slain, a surviving “brother” may remit, and fair payment must then be made to him.

luna: “Life in qisas” states why the retaliation law protects the living, and its address to “people of understanding” echoes the surah’s oath being directed to ذِي حِجْرٍ. | terra: The statement that retaliation contains life gives the section's “my life” its precise legal echo, while the address to people of understanding parallels 89:5's appeal to one possessing discernment.

luna: Within the sacred-month rule, the verse says a violation may be answered in equal measure. Its setting is armed conflict rather than a murdered person’s guardian, but it states the same bounded-return principle. | terra: The rule to answer aggression only in equal measure supplies another explicit Quranic boundary against the escalation natural to blood vengeance.
terra: Every soul will be paid in full for what it earned and none will be wronged, an exact formulation of recompense preserved until the return to God.
terra: On the indisputable Day, every soul is paid in full for what it earned without injustice; no blood claim or deed disappears before account.
terra: In a grave truth dispute, both parties are told to summon sons, women, and themselves and invoke God's curse on the liars; it is a family-involving oath ordeal that transfers judgment to God.
terra: Precedents have passed before the hearers, who are told to travel and inspect the deniers' end; earlier punishment is offered for present deterrence.

luna: The verse warns disbelievers not to mistake their respite for good, since the delay lets them increase in sin before humiliating punishment; it gives a moral reason for the section’s kept account. | terra: The respite given to disbelievers only lets them increase in sin before a humiliating punishment, so delay cannot be mistaken for a lost claim.
terra: God answers that He never lets any worker's work be lost, mentions men and women as “one from another,” and promises those killed a preserved reward.
terra: Believers are forbidden to kill one another, and 4:30 assigns fire to anyone who does so through aggression and injustice.
terra: The unjust aggressor of 4:29 is promised the Fire, carrying communal homicide from human violation into divine punishment.
terra: God does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies a good deed, sharpening both exact liability and generous repayment.

luna: The section’s dictionary note connects the valley word at 89:9 to diyah; this rule explicitly requires دِيَةٌ مُّسَلَّمَةٌ إِلَىٰ أَهْلِهِ, compensation delivered to the slain believer’s family after accidental killing. | terra: The accidental killing rule explicitly requires وَدِيَةٌ مُسَلَّمَةٌ إِلَى أَهْلِهِ, the section's exact secondary sense of the w-d-y root: blood money delivered to the victim's family.

luna: The verse distinguishes deliberate killing of a believer from 4:92’s accidental-killing compensation and names a severe divine recompense. It extends the section’s movement from a human family claim to a penalty no guardian can settle. | terra: Deliberate murder is followed by Hell, divine anger, curse, and a tremendous punishment, moving an earthly blood crime into the Lord's final requital.

luna: The command to testify justly even against oneself, parents, or close relatives is a direct boundary on a kin-based claim: the duty is truthful justice even when the testimony harms one’s own family.

luna: The verse forbids allowing hatred of a people to make one unjust; this is a specific restraint on the vengeance and excess that can attach to a blood claim. | terra: Hatred of a people may not drive believers away from justice, a direct ethical curb on the animus surrounding vengeance for slain kin.

luna: This verse introduces the two sons of Adam whose conflict continues in 5:28–30; that neighboring account supplies the family setting for the refusal and killing named in those following ayat. | terra: The two sons of Adam are introduced as brothers, and one explicitly threatens to kill the other; this establishes the family relation and threatened bloodshed completed in 5:30.

luna: In the story of two brothers, one says he will not extend his hand to kill the other if attacked. That is a specific refusal of reciprocal killing within the very family scene from which blood vengeance arises. | terra: The threatened brother refuses to stretch out his hand to kill even if attacked, a deliberate refusal of reciprocal bloodshed before the fratricide in 5:30.

luna: The threatened brother warns that killing him would bring the other into the company of the Fire; the account locates consequence in divine judgment rather than a human guardian’s retaliation. | terra: Before the fratricide, the threatened brother assigns the killer's burden to him and names the Fire as his requital, anticipating the human killing and divine payment in 5:30.

luna: The story then states that one brother kills the other. This is a direct kin-murder scene beside the section’s imagined murdered relative, though the story proceeds to guilt and burial rather than a blood claim. | terra: The first brother's soul induces him to kill his brother, providing the Quran's stark family-murder scene behind the section's implied slain person and bereaved kin.
terra: The raven teaches the killer how to cover his brother's corpse and he becomes remorseful, supplying the bodily aftermath of the Quran's archetypal family murder.

luna: This prescription to the Children of Israel says that killing a soul without a life-for-life cause is like killing all humanity, while saving one is like saving all. It deepens the section’s claim that qisas has life as its purpose. | terra: The decree following that fratricide equates unjustly killing one soul with killing all people and saving one with saving all, giving the life-preserving boundary behind retaliation.
terra: The thief's penalty is called both recompense for what was earned and a deterrent from God, joining the section's exemplary punishment to exact requital.

luna: The law “a life for a life” and “wounds are subject to qisas” makes measured retaliation explicit, while the same verse also names pardon as an alternative. | terra: “Life for life” and like-for-like retaliation state the measured blood claim, while remission as charity marks the merciful boundary to exact repayment.
terra: One who kills game intentionally owes an equivalent judged by two just persons, joining killing, the m-th-l sense of equivalence, and measured compensation in a different legal domain.

luna: The section links قَسَمٌ to oaths distributed among a slain person’s guardians; here, after a death during travel, two witnesses swear by God about a bequest when doubt arises. The legal setting is a testament rather than homicide, but it is a specific death-linked oath procedure. | terra: At the approach of death, two witnesses are detained and made to swear by God; 5:107 then transfers that oath-bearing role to the nearer claimants if betrayal appears.

luna: The next step in the death-and-bequest procedure replaces witnesses found to have sinned with others who swear by God. This is a distinct legal setting from the section’s qasama, but it shows an oath being used to correct a disputed claim after a death. | terra: When the first witnesses prove untrustworthy, two nearer lawful claimants take their place and swear; this closely parallels a grave right being pursued through oaths allocated to kin.
terra: The threat of counter-oaths after the first oaths is said to discipline testimony, completing 5:106–107's legal scene of death, claimants, and distributed swearing.
terra: The command not to kill a soul except by right repeats the legal boundary around bloodshed while placing it among duties to family and the vulnerable.

luna: The verse says an evil deed is repaid only with its like, while good is multiplied; it distinguishes exact liability from generosity in the divine account. | terra: A good deed is multiplied tenfold while an evil deed is repaid only with its equivalent and no one is wronged, clarifying both preservation and the merciful asymmetry of requital.
terra: No bearer carries another's burden; this individual-liability rule opposes any clan feud that would make a relative answer for the killer's blood debt.
luna: Salih reminds Thamud that they carve houses from mountains after building palaces on the plains; this repeats the specific stone-working image in 89:9.

luna: Shuayb likewise commands full measure and balance and forbids reducing people’s things; it is another concrete formulation of the section’s secondary “diminished right” sense. | terra: The command not to diminish people's goods expresses the human wrong of reducing another's due, against the assurance that God never diminishes earned deeds.
luna: When punishment reaches Pharaoh’s people, they ask Moses to invoke God and promise to believe if it is removed; this begins a concrete account of punishment held pending their response.
luna: After the affliction is removed until an appointed term, Pharaoh’s people break their promise; this ayah shows wrongdoing continuing during reprieve.

luna: The next ayah says God took retribution from them and drowned them, completing the delayed return in Pharaoh’s example. | terra: God takes vengeance on Pharaoh's people by drowning them for denying the signs, another direct case of the section's tyrant receiving divine requital.
terra: Those denying the signs are led gradually from where they do not know, describing a delayed requital that remains active while hidden.
terra: God gives the deniers respite while His plan remains firm, the temporal counterpart of standing at a watchpost until the due time.

luna: The same مرصد root can describe people sitting in ambush at every lookout in a wartime command. That is human tactical waiting, a different and hostile use from the section’s divine watch over an account. | terra: “Lie in wait for them at every marṣad” preserves the literal human ambush behind the section's metaphor of a watcher stationed for what will come.

luna: The mosque built as إِرْصَادًا is a human ambush serving opposition to God and His Messenger; this other use of the section’s ر ص د root makes the moral difference from the Lord’s just waiting matter. | terra: A building is prepared as an irṣād, an outpost for one who fought God and His messenger; this corrupt human station reverses the Lord's just watchpost of recompense.
terra: Every valley the believers cross is written for them so God may reward them; the literal wādī unexpectedly meets the section's separate motif of recompense kept on record.

luna: The verse uses the section’s م ث ل root for evil repaid with its like, giving a direct Qur’anic wording for measured recompense. | terra: An evil deed receives a recompense like it, using the m-th-l root for exact equivalence rather than the exemplary punishment sense developed in the section.
terra: No deed and not even an atom's weight escapes the Lord, and all is in a clear record; this specifies how held recompense cannot disappear.

luna: The delayed punishment is questioned as though something were holding it back, but when it comes nothing turns it aside; this closely develops the section’s image of a return held ready at the mirsad.

terra: Those seeking only worldly life are paid their works there without diminution, but the following ayah denies them an afterlife share; it marks the boundary between immediate payment and lasting recompense.
luna: After Thamud hamstring the she-camel, they are given only three days’ respite before the promised punishment; this is a particularly concrete instance of the section’s recompense held in wait.
luna: The next punishment account says a cry seized the wrongdoers; it completes the three-day warning given in 11:65.

luna: The section’s secondary dictionary form for وَتَرَ is “to reduce his right”; Shuʿayb similarly forbids بِخْس, reducing people’s due in measure. The domain is trade rather than blood compensation, but the concrete wrong is the same deprivation of what is owed. | terra: Full measure and weight are required and people's goods may not be diminished, another concrete form of withholding a right.
terra: God's seizure of wrongdoing towns is painful and severe, a general statement distilled from the exemplary destructions surrounding the section's named peoples.
terra: The Lord will pay every person fully for their deeds because He knows what they do, directly restating the section's kept recompense.
terra: God does not let the reward of those who do good be lost, another exact formulation of beneficence held until repayment.

terra: The brothers bring false blood on Joseph's shirt to persuade their father that a family member was killed; it is a specific inversion of a true blood claim, though no homicide or lawful oath occurred.
terra: The stories of earlier peoples contain a lesson for people of understanding, joining exemplary history to the discerning addressee invoked by the section's oath.

luna: The source section’s dictionary branch on م ث ل describes a punishment made an example; this verse says earlier مُثُلَات had already passed before those demanding evil quickly, supplying the direct Qur’anic formulation. | terra: The deniers demand evil before good although ٱلْمَثُلَاتُ, exemplary punishments, have already passed before them; this is the exact punitive sense developed from 89:8.

luna: God is not unaware of wrongdoers; He only postpones them to a day when eyes stare. This directly explains the section’s waiting image as deferred, not forgotten, recompense. | terra: God is not heedless of wrongdoers but only delays them to a fixed day, the temporal posture of a Lord stationed in wait for account.
terra: At the arrival of punishment, the wrongdoers are reminded that they had sworn they would never pass away; 14:45 then places them among ruined predecessors and examples.
terra: The audience lived in the dwellings of earlier wrongdoers, saw how God dealt with them, and received examples; past punishment is made present as deterrence.
terra: God never breaks His promise to the messengers and is possessor of vengeance; after 14:42's delay, requital is certain rather than forgotten.
terra: God takes vengeance on the two offending communities and leaves both sites visible on a clear road, making their punishment a standing warning.
luna: The section singles out Thamud cutting rock in the valley; here the people of al-Hijr carve houses into mountains while feeling secure, a close recurrence of their rock-cut dwelling scene.
luna: The next ayah says a cry seized the mountain-house builders in the morning, giving one of the section’s named exemplary peoples a concrete punishment.
luna: The following verse says what they had earned did not avail them; it adds the failure of their worldly works to the Thamud punishment example.

luna: God does not immediately seize people for their wrongdoing, but postpones them to a stated term; when it arrives, it cannot be delayed. This is a specific parallel to recompense held until its appointed time.
luna: “What is with you passes, but what is with God remains” directly develops the section’s claim that the return is not lost but stays in place; the verse then promises recompense to the patient.
terra: Each soul comes pleading for itself and is paid fully for what it did without injustice, placing exact repayment in the final court.
terra: God presents a secure, well-provided town as an example and then clothes it in hunger and fear for ingratitude, making communal punishment into a warning image.

luna: If retaliation is taken, this verse limits it to the harm received, then says patience is better; it gives the section’s blood-return image an explicit boundary and alternative. | terra: If people retaliate, they may do so only to the measure inflicted on them, while patience is better; this is the exact limit that keeps a blood claim from excess.
luna: Every person’s record is attached to them and opened on the Day of Resurrection; this makes the section’s preserved account an individual, unavoidable record.
luna: The next ayah tells each person to read their record and says they suffice as their own reckoner, clarifying that no guardian can settle the final account for them.

luna: This is the section’s precise guardian-and-limit counterpart: the wrongfully slain person’s ولي is given authority, but is forbidden to exceed the bounds in killing. It distinguishes justice for a victim from a new blood excess. | terra: The guardian of one wrongfully killed receives authority, but may not exceed the limit in killing; it both stages the section's bereaved claimant and confines blood vengeance.
terra: God does not let the reward of anyone who does good work be lost, a direct nonlexical equivalent of keeping beneficence until repayment.

luna: The opened record leaves out neither small nor great deeds; it makes the section’s “the return does not disappear” claim visible as an account with no omissions. | terra: The record omits neither small nor great and people find their deeds present; this makes concrete the section's claim that recompense stays in place until account.
terra: Moses objects to killing a pure soul “not in retaliation for a soul,” stating the life-for-life boundary precisely by protesting its apparent breach.
terra: The messenger is told not to hasten against the wrongdoers because God is counting out their term exactly, combining delay, surveillance, and certain reckoning.
terra: God recalls that Moses killed a person, was rescued from distress, and was tried through trials, compressing homicide and its feared aftermath into one divine account.

luna: The just scales do not wrong a soul even by a mustard-seed weight; this gives exact measure to the section’s claim that recompense is kept rather than lost. | terra: Just scales are set, no soul is wronged, and even a mustard-seed weight is brought forth, portraying exact requital held until the final reckoning.
terra: Noah's people, ʿĀd, and Thamud are grouped as prior deniers, beginning a warning list whose delayed seizure is stated in 22:44.
terra: After adding Moses to the rejected messengers, God says He granted the deniers respite and then seized them, a precise sequence of watchful delay and requital.

luna: The verse allows one harmed to answer in like measure and promises divine help if that person is wronged again, a specific parallel for measured response and the Lord’s role beyond human claimants. | terra: One who answers injury with its equal and is then attacked is promised God's help, combining measured retaliation with the Lord's ultimate redress.
terra: A group of believers must witness the prescribed punishment, making the penalty publicly visible in the manner of an exemplary deterrent.

luna: In a different family-law case, a husband answers an accusation with four sworn testimonies and a fifth invoking God’s curse if he lies. This is a specific parallel to the section’s oath procedure among a murdered person’s guardians, though it concerns an accusation between spouses. | terra: A husband with no witnesses in a grave family accusation supplies four sworn attestations himself; it is a close legal analogue to using apportioned oaths when ordinary proof is absent.

luna: This ayah supplies the husband’s fifth oath and its consequence, continuing the fixed family testimony procedure begun in 24:6. | terra: The husband's fifth invocation places God's curse on him if he lies, giving the oath procedure an explicitly deferred divine sanction.

luna: The wife may avert the prescribed penalty by giving four sworn testimonies against her husband’s charge; the oath procedure turns to the accused family member’s answer. | terra: The wife averts the legal punishment through four counter-attestations by God, so opposed family claims are bounded by balanced oath-taking rather than private violence.

luna: The fifth testimony invokes God’s wrath if the husband is truthful, closing the reciprocal oath procedure in this distinct family-law setting. | terra: Her fifth invocation places God's wrath on her if the husband is truthful, returning the unresolved family claim to divine recompense.
terra: Noah's people are drowned, made a sign for humanity, and assigned a prepared punishment, explicitly joining exemplary destruction to recompense held ready.
terra: ʿĀd and Thamud are inserted into the same catalogue of destroyed peoples, repeating two of the section's named examples.
terra: Examples were set forth to each listed people and each was utterly destroyed, stating why the catalogue in 25:37–38 functions as warning.
terra: The servants of the Merciful neither kill a soul God has made inviolable except by right nor commit other grave crimes; the ayah states the homicide boundary before its divine penalty.
terra: The murderer's punishment is multiplied and made abiding and humiliating, shifting the blood crime of 25:68 into a requital beyond a human guardian's power.
terra: Repentance, faith, and good work can transform evil deeds into good, a merciful reversal to 25:69's otherwise multiplied requital.
terra: Moses says Pharaoh's people hold a blood charge against him and he fears they will kill him, a direct narrative of an unpaid killing generating threatened vengeance.
terra: Pharaoh confronts Moses with the killing he committed, showing that the old blood charge remains remembered before Moses answers in 26:20–21.
terra: Moses acknowledges committing the act while unaware of its course, supplying his own account of the killing invoked by Pharaoh.
terra: Moses says he fled in fear after the killing and was later granted judgment and messengerhood, showing the blood claim's human danger and a different divine resolution.
luna: Thamud are asked whether they carve houses from mountains proudly; it gives another explicit formulation of the rock-cutting that marks the section’s example.
luna: The Thamud narrative says they hamstrung the she-camel; this supplies the specific transgression preceding the exemplary punishment of a people the section names.
luna: The next ayah says punishment seized them, completing that act-to-recompense sequence for Thamud.

luna: Shuayb begins by ordering full measure and forbidding short measure; this is the positive counterpart to reducing another’s right, the secondary sense developed from the section’s وَتَرَهُ حَقَّهُ.
luna: The next ayah commands weighing with a straight balance, completing the measure-and-right scene before 26:183 forbids reducing people’s due.

luna: This command not to reduce people’s things repeats the section’s dictionary sense of a right made short, here in a warning against commercial fraud and corruption. | terra: The people are forbidden to diminish others' goods and spread corruption, stating in social terms the deprivation named by the section's secondary w-t-r sense.
terra: Salih asks Thamud why they hasten evil before good, almost exactly restaging 13:6's demand for punishment before mercy within one of the section's named peoples.
terra: God tells the reader to see the outcome of Thamud's plot: He destroys them and their people, turning their scheme into visible requital.
terra: Their houses lie ruined for their wrongdoing and are declared a sign for people who know, explicitly making 27:51's punishment exemplary.
terra: Moses strikes a man and unintentionally causes his death, a narrative instance against which 4:92's accidental-killing compensation can be understood.
terra: Moses immediately confesses wrong and receives forgiveness, showing divine pardon in the accidental killing scene while 4:92 states the surviving family's earthly due.
terra: A man exposes Moses by asking whether he means to kill him as he killed someone the previous day, making the concealed homicide publicly actionable.
terra: A man warns Moses that the chiefs are plotting to kill him and urges flight, showing the retaliatory consequence of the killing reaching him.
terra: Moses says he killed one of Pharaoh's people and fears they will kill him, explicitly staging the reciprocal blood claim latent in the section's vetr imagery.

luna: Evil is repaid only with its like, while good receives better; this is a concise statement of the proportional account the section hears in mirsad. | terra: Whoever brings good receives better, while evil-doers receive only the like of what they did; the m-th-l root again marks measured repayment with merciful asymmetry.

luna: This ayah names Ad and Thamud and points to their dwellings, recalling the same earlier peoples whose transgression and punishment the section treats as precedents. | terra: ʿĀd and Thamud are recalled through dwellings still visible to the hearers, so their destroyed societies remain concrete warning-examples.

luna: The next ayah brings in Pharaoh among arrogant people who rejected clear proofs; the following 29:40 completes their seizure, so this is the named Pharaoh contribution to that punishment sequence.

luna: The verse says each group was seized for its sin by a fitting mode and that God did not wrong them; this is a concise account of the section’s precedent punishments and just return. | terra: Each earlier people is seized for its sin by wind-borne stones, blast, earth-collapse, or drowning; the varied penalties complete 29:38's exemplary catalogue.

luna: The verse says corruption appeared on land and sea because of what people’s hands earned, so they taste some of their deeds. This directly joins the section’s corrupting peoples to the punishment poured upon them.
terra: God sent messengers with proofs, took vengeance on the criminals, and declares support of believers His due, combining historical requital and preserved right.
terra: Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in rock, heaven, or earth is brought forth by God, making the “not lost” claim spatially vivid.
terra: God declares that He takes vengeance upon criminals who turn from His signs, locating final redress in the divine claimant.
terra: No burdened soul can transfer any load even to a close relative, a family-specific bar against collective liability in a blood feud.
luna: If God took people at once for what they earned, no creature would remain, but He postpones them to a term; the verse makes the section’s watchful delay explicit.
terra: No soul is wronged at all on that day and people are repaid only for what they did, a concise account of measured divine requital.
terra: The deniers ask to hasten God's punishment, repeating the impatience for evil before good named in the section.
terra: When punishment descends into their courtyard, the warned people's morning will be terrible, answering 37:176's demand with the awaited event.
terra: A single catalogue joins Noah's people, ʿĀd, and Pharaoh “of the stakes”; 38:13 adds Thamud and 38:14 states that punishment became due.
terra: Thamud is added to the same exemplary roll as ʿĀd and Pharaoh in 38:12, preparing 38:14's common verdict.
terra: Each listed people denied the messengers, so God's punishment came due; the ayah supplies the shared requital that makes 38:12–13's nations examples.
terra: The record, prophets, and witnesses are brought and judgment is made in truth without injustice; 39:70 then states the full payment to every soul.
terra: Every soul is paid fully for what it did after the record and witnesses are brought, so the final judgment leaves no claim unpaid.
luna: Every soul is repaid for what it earned and no one is wronged; this is the precise reckoning behind the section’s image of a return held ready.
terra: The believing man in Pharaoh's house warns of a fate “like” that of Noah's people, ʿĀd, and Thamud, using earlier destroyed peoples to deter Pharaoh from injustice.
terra: An evil deed receives only its like, while righteous good receives provision without measure; exact liability and overflowing grace distinguish two forms of divine repayment.

luna: Pharaoh’s people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, then commanded into the harsher punishment when the Hour comes; the interval directly evokes the section’s punishment held ready at the mirsad.

luna: This warning invokes a lightning strike like that of Ad and Thamud, showing those same peoples serving as prior punishment examples for another audience. | terra: The audience is warned of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamud, directly turning their punishments into a threatened precedent.
luna: Ad’s punishment is described as a violent wind and humiliating chastisement in worldly life and the next, developing one of the section’s named exemplary peoples.
luna: Thamud reject guidance and are seized by the humiliating lightning punishment; this supplies the same kind of exemplary return for the other named people.
luna: The next ayah says the believers were saved; its own contribution is the boundary between those seized in the punishment and those delivered.

luna: “The recompense of an injury is an injury like it,” followed by pardon and reconciliation, directly joins equivalent return to the alternative of mercy that bounds the section’s vendetta image. | terra: An injury may be repaid only with its like, but pardon and reconciliation move the claimant's reward to God; this directly illuminates measured vengeance and a recompense kept by the Lord.
terra: When Pharaoh's people provoke God, He takes vengeance and drowns them all; divine requital produces the example named in the next ayah.
terra: God makes Pharaoh's people a precedent and “an example for the later ones,” the clearest parallel to the section's past peoples preserved as deterrent punishments.
terra: On the day of the greatest seizure God declares “We will take vengeance,” locating the final blood-debt vocabulary in divine judgment.

luna: This verse likewise says each soul is recompensed for its earning without injustice, spelling out the moral account implied by the Lord’s mirsad. | terra: Creation in truth serves a judgment in which each soul is repaid for what it earned and none is wronged, matching the section's assured counterpayment.
terra: Every person has degrees according to deeds so God may pay them fully, with no injustice; earned differences are preserved until recompense.

luna: Ad see a cloud approaching their valleys and take it for rain, but it is the painful wind they had been promised. This specific reversal deepens the section’s use of Ad as an example of punishment rather than benefit.
luna: The following ayah says the wind destroyed everything by its Lord’s command, leaving only the dwellings visible; it completes the cloud-to-punishment reversal.
terra: The hearers are told to inspect the end of earlier peoples whom God destroyed, with “the like of it” awaiting disbelievers; exemplary past and promised counterpart meet.

luna: The section explicitly glosses its source form وَتَرَهُ حَقَّهُ as reducing someone’s right, and cites يَتِرَكُمْ here: in its battle exhortation God promises not to diminish the believers’ deeds, the divine opposite of an unpaid or reduced due. | terra: وَلَن يَتِرَكُمْ أَعْمَالَكُمْ uses the section's w-t-r root in its “diminish a right” sense and promises that God will subtract nothing from the believers' deeds.
terra: God will not diminish anything from the believers' deeds, restating without w-t-r the precise assurance expressed by 47:35 and the section's claim that requital is not lost.
terra: Noah's people, the people of the well, and Thamud begin another catalogue of communities that denied before the present hearers.
terra: ʿĀd and Pharaoh are added to the catalogue containing Thamud, again gathering the section's exemplary peoples.
terra: Every listed people denied the messengers, so God's threatened punishment became due; the verdict makes 50:12–13's names punitive examples.

luna: An observer ready is assigned to each spoken word; it parallels the section’s watchman image by making human acts continuously observed before their accounting. | terra: Every utterance meets an observer standing ready, a concrete account scene in which nothing passes the waiting watcher unrecorded.
terra: After the opening oaths, the speaker declares the promised event true; 51:6 identifies that promise as certain requital.
terra: The oath sequence culminates in “the recompense will surely occur,” matching this section's movement from oath to a Lord holding payment ready.
terra: A sequence of oaths culminates in the certainty of the Lord's punishment, reproducing the section's structural passage from sworn signs to requital.
terra: “No one can avert it” gives 52:7's divine punishment the unmatched finality heard beside 89:25.
terra: God joins believing descendants to their family and diminishes nothing from their work, combining the family image with the preservation of every earned right.
terra: God owns all that is in heaven and earth so He may repay evildoers for their deeds and reward good-doers with the best, joining both sides of the watchpost image.
luna: A person has only what they strove for; this sharply individualizes the deeds whose return the section says is not diminished.
luna: The following ayah says that striving will be seen, extending the personal account from action to disclosure.
luna: Then each person is repaid fully; this is a precise parallel to the section’s promise that the due return remains intact.

luna: Ad’s denial is followed by the question of how the punishment and warnings were; this repeated warning formula makes one of the section’s examples explicitly didactic. | terra: ʿĀd denies, and the surrounding refrain asks the reader to consider God's punishment and warnings, explicitly presenting the people as a deterrent case.
terra: After ʿĀd's destruction, the refrain again asks how God's punishment and warnings were, fixing the episode's exemplary function.

luna: Thamud’s denial is likewise followed by the warning about punishment; it develops the section’s precedent-punishment image around its other named people. | terra: Thamud denies the warnings, beginning a parallel exemplary cycle immediately after the ʿĀd cycle.
terra: The Thamud cycle ends with the same question about God's punishment and warnings, marking its destruction as another deterrent example.
terra: Warnings reach Pharaoh's people, introducing the third of the section's named civilizations into the repeated pattern.

luna: Pharaoh’s people denied the signs and were seized; this is a direct narrative counterpart to the section’s naming Pharaoh among the exemplary punished. | terra: Pharaoh's people deny all the signs and are seized by One mighty and fully able, supplying the unmatched requital that completes 54:41.
terra: “Is the recompense of excellence anything but excellence?” directly matches the dictionary explanation of keeping another's good until it can be repaid.
terra: The divine speaker swears by the settings of the stars, introducing the explicitly named qasam of 56:76.
terra: The oath is called a tremendous قَسَم “if you knew,” closely paralleling 89:5's question whether its oath is sufficient for a discerning mind.
terra: After an unexpected communal punishment, the hearers are commanded to take warning, explicitly turning a historical downfall into an example for perceptive people.
terra: The deniers are asked whether they possess binding oaths from God lasting until Judgment that guarantee whatever they decide, exposing a false claim to control the final award.
terra: God tells the messenger to leave the deniers to Him while He draws them gradually from where they do not know, another image of personally reserved requital.

luna: This ayah names Thamud and Ad as deniers of the striking calamity, setting up the distinct punishments narrated for them in 69:5–8. | terra: Thamud and ʿĀd jointly deny the overwhelming judgment, opening another compact catalogue of the section's warning-peoples.

luna: This account says Thamud were destroyed by the overwhelming blast, a concrete instance of the earlier exemplary punishments the section names. | terra: Thamud is destroyed by the overwhelming blast, giving the first specific exemplary penalty in the catalogue.

luna: The same account says Ad were destroyed by a furious wind, making another of the section’s named exempla an actual punishment scene. | terra: ʿĀd is destroyed by a furious wind, placing its distinct requital beside Thamud's.
luna: The next account specifies that Ad’s wind lasted seven nights and eight days, giving duration and physical force to the punishment of a people named in the section.
luna: The account asks whether any remnant of Ad can be seen after the wind, completing the example as a destruction that leaves no people behind.

luna: Here Pharaoh and the overturned cities are named among those who came with wrongdoing, carrying the section’s Pharaoh example into a wider account of punished communities. | terra: Pharaoh and the overturned towns are added to the same sequence of peoples who brought grave offenses.

luna: The next ayah says they disobeyed their Lord’s messenger and He seized them with an overwhelming seizure, specifying the recompense attached to 69:9’s named offenders. | terra: Their disobedience is answered by a surpassing seizure, stating the recompense common to 69:4–9's examples.
terra: The preserved ark is made a reminder received by an attentive ear, explicitly stating why scenes of past punishment and rescue are kept before later hearers.
terra: A questioner demands the punishment that will fall, repeating the section's motif of people impatiently summoning evil.
terra: The demanded punishment belongs to the disbelievers and has no one able to repel it, giving divine requital the finality heard beside 89:25.
terra: The unrepellable punishment comes from God, locating the claim above every human avenger.

luna: On the Day described here, a close friend does not ask after another; this reverses the section’s earthly image of a slain person’s kin pressing a claim, as final recompense exceeds their reach.
luna: A person can see those close to him yet wish to ransom himself from the punishment; this develops the limit that a guardian cannot perform or avert the ultimate return.
luna: The passage names wife and brother among the relatives who cannot serve as a substitute in that reckoning, a direct family boundary on the section’s human-wali image.
luna: It expands the unavailable substitute to the clan that sheltered a person, sharpening the difference between human kinship and divine recompense.
luna: The person would offer everyone on earth to be saved; no human substitute can meet the punishment described in the section’s final turn.
terra: An eavesdropper finds a flame lying in wait, a supernatural r-s-d ambush that supplies the spatial sense of the section's divine watchpost.

luna: This verse uses رَصَدًا for watchers placed before and behind a chosen messenger. It develops the watchfulness sense of the section’s mirsad, though here the watchers guard a message rather than await recompense. | terra: God places a guard before and behind a chosen messenger; this uses r-s-d for literal watchers whose purpose is explained through encompassing knowledge and counting in 72:28.

luna: The neighboring verse says God encompasses what they have and counts everything; it adds exact enumeration to the messenger-guarding scene and to the section’s claim that nothing due is lost. | terra: God encompasses the messengers and counts everything exactly, completing 72:27's r-s-d guard scene with the account-like enumeration sensed in the section's watchpost.
terra: The speaker commands that the prosperous deniers be left to Him and granted a little respite, the posture of a Lord personally holding their case until payment.
terra: The reason for leaving the deniers to God is that shackles and a blazing fire are with Him, an unmatched penalty already held ready.
terra: Choking food and painful punishment complete the prepared recompense announced in 73:11–12.
luna: Each soul is held to what it earned; this contrasts the family’s human effort to claim blood with personal divine liability that cannot be shifted to another.
terra: After a chain of divine oaths, the promised event is declared inevitable, a structural parallel to this section's oath leading toward stored requital.

luna: The word مِرْصَادًا repeats the section’s 89:14 word: here Hell is lying in wait, making the watch-and-recompense image concrete. | terra: إِنَّ جَهَنَّمَ كَانَتْ مِرْصَادًا repeats the watchpost noun and makes Hell itself the waiting station of recompense.

luna: The next ayah identifies the ones for whom the 78:21 mirsad waits: the transgressors. That supplies the target of the waiting image in the cited verse. | terra: The watchpost of 78:21 is specifically a destination for transgressors, identifying whom the waiting station receives.

luna: The same passage calls the punishment جَزَاءً وِفَاقًا, a fitting recompense; this is a direct formulation of the measured return kept ready in the section. | terra: The punishment at the watchpost is “a fitting recompense,” stating the measured payment that 78:21's scene holds ready.
terra: The reason given is that they did not expect an account, making explicit the reckoning that the section says the watcher awaits.

luna: God seizes Pharaoh as نَكَال, a punishment made an example, directly joining the section’s Pharaoh exemplar to the dictionary sense of exemplary penalty. | terra: God seizes Pharaoh with an exemplary punishment for his latter and former offense, making the section's named tyrant a deterrent instance.

luna: The following ayah calls that event a lesson for those who fear, stating explicitly what the section’s exemplary punishments are for. | terra: The verse declares Pharaoh's fate in 79:25 a lesson for whoever fears, explicitly turning punishment into the warning-example perceived by a receptive hearer.
terra: On Judgment Day the murdered girl herself is summoned as the claimant; 81:9 voices the question that ensures her otherwise hidden blood is not lost.
terra: “For what sin was she killed?” makes an unavenged victim's case present before God, where the section's final requital exceeds what any human guardian supplied.
luna: The passage says watchers are set over people, beginning a scene of deeds being observed that parallels the section’s Lord at the mirsad.
luna: The next ayah identifies those watchers as noble recorders, specifying that observation becomes a preserved record.
luna: The following ayah says they know what people do, completing the record-and-recompense parallel.

luna: The opening woe names the mutaffifin, the underweighers; the next two ayat specify their practice of taking full measure and giving less, a concrete instance of the right-reduction named in the section. | terra: Woe is announced to those who give short measure, introducing a systematic human practice of diminishing others' rights that 83:2–3 specifies.

luna: These traders take their measure in full for themselves, establishing the one-sided exchange that the section’s language of diminished rights makes perceptible. | terra: The defrauders demand full measure when receiving from others, showing the claimant's insistence on an undiminished due.

luna: When they measure or weigh for others, they give less; this is a precise transactional picture of withholding what is due. | terra: When measuring or weighing for others, the defrauders cause loss, the precise reversal of God's promise not to diminish works.

luna: The passage asks whether these underweighers expect to be raised, explicitly joining the reduced measure in 83:1–3 to future reckoning. | terra: The defrauders are asked whether they expect to be resurrected, connecting hidden diminution of rights to the coming account.
luna: The next ayah identifies the accounting horizon as a great day, completing the fraud-to-recompense link.
luna: People stand before the Lord of the worlds on that day; this gives the underweighers’ present short measure the future accounting that the section names as the Lord’s mirsad.
luna: The passage about underweighers continues by placing the record of the wicked in Sijjin, tying the short measure in 83:1–3 to a preserved adverse account.
luna: This ayah identifies Sijjin as a written record, specifying how the wicked traders’ account is kept.
luna: The other side of the surah says the record of the righteous is in Illiyyun, a direct counterpart to the wicked record and to the section’s assurance that good deeds are not lost.
luna: The ayah calls Illiyyun a written record, specifying preservation for the righteous as the passage did for the wicked.
luna: The next ayah says those brought near witness that record, completing the preserved account of good deeds.

luna: The surah ends by asking whether the disbelievers have been recompensed for what they did; this is an explicit question of deferred return, though its immediate context is those who mocked believers.
luna: The person given their record in the right hand faces an account; this develops the section’s preserved deeds into a personal reckoning.
luna: The following ayah says that person receives an easy accounting, clarifying the outcome of the record in 84:7.
luna: The next ayah says the person returns to their family rejoicing; this adds a family scene to the section’s final movement from judgment toward a welcomed return.
luna: The person given the record from behind faces the other side of the account, a specific contrast to the return and approval at the end of the section.
luna: The next ayah says this person calls for destruction, completing the adverse record’s immediate consequence.
luna: The following ayah says they enter the Blaze, completing the adverse outcome paired with the record in 84:10.
terra: The Lord's seizure is declared severe, reinforcing the claim that final divine punishment surpasses a human guardian's retaliation.
terra: The hearer is asked whether the story of the hosts has reached him, introducing Pharaoh and Thamud as remembered warning forces.
terra: Pharaoh and Thamud are named together as the hosts whose story 85:17 invokes, repeating two of the section's exemplary peoples.
terra: God encompasses the deniers from behind, a spatial parallel to the watchpost's inescapable oversight after the Pharaoh-and-Thamud reminder.
terra: God inflicts “the greatest punishment” on the one who turns away, a close parallel to the final penalty no human avenger can perform.
terra: The return of all people is to God, locating the unmatched punishment of 88:24 in the divine rather than familial forum.
terra: Their account belongs to God, completing 88:24–25 with the reckoning awaited at the section's watchpost.
terra: Thamud denies Salih, kills the she-camel, and is crushed by the Lord for its sin, another direct instance of the named people becoming exemplary punishment.
terra: God does not fear the consequence of leveling Thamud, underscoring how divine requital exceeds the constraints and vulnerability of a human avenger.

luna: The tiniest good is seen, a direct counterpart to the section’s assurance that a person’s deed will not be diminished or lost. | terra: Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, a concise statement that beneficence remains available for repayment.

luna: The following verse gives the matching result for the tiniest evil, completing the account on the adverse side of the section’s reckoning. | terra: Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it, extending the watchpost image from preserved reward to unavoidable penalty.
